scenario: You’ve spent an hour fixing a CSS bug with Copilot. Now you need help writing a SQL migration.

options.text: Ask in the same chat; Copilot already knows the project.
Type /clear and start the migration in a fresh chat.
Use /compact, then ask about the migration.

why: Unrelated work gets a new chat. The CSS history would be re-sent and billed with every migration prompt and could steer answers. /compact is for staying on the same task.

scenario: Same feature, two hours in. The context window control is at 70% and you still need the API decisions you made early on.

options.text: Keep going; VS Code will compact automatically.
/compact keep the API decisions and open questions
/clear and start over from scratch.

why: A focused /compact keeps what you choose. Automatic compaction keeps whatever it guesses, and /clear would lose decisions you still need.

scenario: Your build failed with a 1,500-line log in the terminal. How do you get help?

options.text: Copy the whole log into the chat.
Select the error lines and use #terminalSelection, or #terminalLastCommand.
Describe the error from memory.

why: Reference the output instead of pasting it, and select only the relevant lines when you can. The whole log costs tokens on every later prompt too.

scenario: Copilot has got the same function wrong twice, even after your corrections.

options.text: Correct it a third time, more firmly.
Switch to the largest model and keep going in this chat.
/clear and write a better prompt with the constraint it kept missing.

why: The wrong attempts are now in the context and keep pulling it back. A fresh chat with a clearer prompt usually fixes it, and costs less than a big model on a polluted history.

scenario: You need to rename a prop across five components.

options.text: Pick the most powerful reasoning model to be safe.
Leave the model on Auto, or use a rename refactor (F2) if the editor can do it.
Use Plan mode first.

why: Routine work doesn’t need an expensive model, and the editor’s own rename is free and exact. Save big models and planning for hard problems.

scenario: You need to add audit logging across eight services and you’re not sure of the approach.

options.text: Agent: “Add audit logging everywhere.”
Plan first: list files, order and risks, then implement step by step in Agent.
Ask: “What is audit logging?”

why: Fixing a plan costs a few lines; undoing a wide, wrong agent run costs a lot of tokens and time.

scenario: You type “use our logger, not console.log” in nearly every prompt.

options.text: Add it to .github/copilot-instructions.md once.
Keep typing it; it works.
Write a 500-line style guide into the instructions file.

why: Instruction files are applied automatically. But they’re sent on every request, so keep them short and to the point.

scenario: A test fails because of a bad API key. You want Copilot’s help.

options.text: Paste the .env file so it can see the key.
Share the error and the code that reads the key, with the value replaced by a placeholder.
Turn on auto-approve so the agent can read .env itself.

why: Secrets never go into prompts. Copilot doesn’t need the value to fix how it’s loaded.

scenario: Your admin has set content exclusion for /payments. You run Agent mode on a nearby feature.

options.text: The agent can’t read /payments, so you don’t need to think about it.
Content exclusion isn’t supported in Agent mode, so keep the agent away from /payments and watch its file reads.

why: GitHub’s docs say content exclusion doesn’t apply in Edit and Agent modes. Don’t rely on it there.

scenario: The agent finished and says “All tests pass.”

options.text: Keep the changes and commit.
Check the test output yourself, read the diff, then commit.

why: Trust, but verify. Read every change and see the real test result before it goes anywhere.
